title: Do I Have to Be a Jerk to Succeed?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece pushes back on the popular assumption that success and bad character travel together. It acknowledges that some highly successful and talented people behave badly, but argues that visibility, not correlation, explains the perception — successful jerks simply make better stories and get more attention than quietly decent high performers. The article separates talent and success from character entirely, insisting neither requires the other and that treating bad behavior as the price of admission for greatness lets accomplished people get away with conduct that would never be tolerated from anyone else. It closes by reframing how people treat others as a fully learned, chosen set of behaviors, independent of accomplishment.
points: The correlation between talent/success and good character is lower than assumed, but the piece argues visibility — not frequency — explains why "successful jerks" seem common.
Society often gives highly accomplished people a pass for selfish or scandalous behavior specifically because their talent is so alluring.
The article insists success and character are only "yoked when we require them to be," rejecting the idea that bad behavior is a necessary cost of achievement.
How a person treats others is framed as an entirely learned and chosen set of behaviors, unrelated to their level of talent or success.
quotes: There are so many highly profile jerks in the world that some people presume you can’t be successful without being a skunk.
Success and character are yoked when we require them to be and too often that is not the case.
Because we find success and talent so alluring, we give the most accomplished jerks a pass.
The real news is that becoming highly successful doesn’t make you a person of quality or stop you from being one.
So don’t be fooled. How you treat others is entirely a learned set of behaviors.
